claims.text: Cryo-rolling followed by annealing can overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength.
The untreated starting alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The proposed intervention is cryo-rolling followed by annealing.
The proposed mechanical-property assessment applies at room temperature.
Cryo-rolling and annealing produce a hierarchical microstructure containing fine lamellar regions and coarse non-lamellar regions.

The fine lamellar regions contain ultrafine FCC grains and B2 lamellae, while the coarse non-lamellar regions contain ultrafine and some coarse FCC grains together with relatively coarse unrecrystallized B2.
Strain partitioning among the constituent phases changes the driving force for recrystallization.
Differences in phase-level strain partitioning generate the complex hierarchical microstructure.
The hierarchical microstructure simultaneously enhances strength and ductility.
The treated material will have yield strength greater than 1400 MPa.
The treated material will have elongation to failure greater than 10%.
The strength and ductility improvements are relative to both as-cast and cold-rolled-and-annealed material.
Applicability is limited by alloy composition and processing conditions.
The exact strain-partitioning mechanism and its effect on properties are not fully understood.
Tensile testing and microstructural analysis can test the hypothesis by measuring yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation to failure, and microstructure.
The hypothesis is falsified if the treated samples do not show significantly higher yield strength and elongation to failure than the as-cast or cold-rolled-and-annealed controls.
